analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run health plan covering everyone in the US, replacing private health insurance.
analysis.headline: The Medicare for All bill attracted 62 House Democratic cosponsors but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in its two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put every US resident on a single public health plan covering doctor visits, hospital care, prescription drugs, dental, vision, hearing, mental health, and long-term care with no deductibles or copays. It would pay for this by pooling the money the government already spends on Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP, plus new taxes on the top 5% of earners, payroll income, investment income, and stock and bond trades. Private insurers could no longer sell coverage that duplicates the public plan, and for-profit hospitals would have to convert to nonprofit status.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who currently pays premiums, deductibles, or copays, or who is uninsured or underinsured, would get comprehensive coverage at no point of service cost. People who lose jobs would keep coverage automatically, since it is tied to residency, not employment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone paying premiums, deductibles, or copays

how_it_helps.text: Every US resident would be covered for all medically necessary care, including dental, vision, hearing aids, mental health, and long-term care, with no deductibles, copayments, or coinsurance [S2] [S3].

The program would be financed with money the government already spends on Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP, plus new taxes on the top 5% of income earners, payroll and self-employment income, unearned income, and stock and bond transactions [S2] [S3].

Insurance and billing paperwork would be sharply reduced, and displaced clerical and billing workers would get first priority in retraining plus two years of salary-parity transition benefits up to $100,000 a year [S2] [S3].
Patients could keep any private doctor or hospital in the program, and could keep medical records out of the electronic system if they chose [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Higher-income households would pay substantially more in taxes on income, payroll, investments, and stock and bond trades. Private health insurers would lose most of their business, for-profit hospitals would have to convert to nonprofit status with owners compensated over 15 years, and drug makers would lose pricing power to bulk government negotiation.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners, insurers, for-profit hospitals, drug makers

drawbacks.text: The plan is financed with new broad-based taxes, including a payroll and self-employment excise tax and a tax on stock and bond transactions, and the bill leaves the exact rates blank for Congress to fill in later [S2] [S3].

Private insurers would be banned from selling coverage that duplicates the public plan, ending the private health insurance industry as it exists; the bill acknowledges the jobs this eliminates by funding two years of transition benefits for clerical and billing workers [S2] [S3].
For-profit hospitals would be required to convert to nonprofit status, with owners compensated for financial losses over a 15-year period through Treasury bonds [S3].
Prescription drug prices would be negotiated annually by the program and a formulary would promote generics, limiting drug makers' current pricing power [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades the entire system of premiums, deductibles, and networks for a single tax-funded plan with no cost-sharing, and its tax design shifts the burden toward high earners and investment income. The genuine costs are the new taxes replacing what people currently pay employers and insurers, the roughly two-year disruption for hundreds of thousands of insurance and billing jobs the bill itself anticipates, and the fact that key tax rates and payment levels are left to be negotiated after passage. An honest supporter would call this the most sweeping health financing change ever proposed; the benefit side is near-universal coverage, the cost side is concentrated and visible.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2015 and split among three House committees, and in the two years before that Congress ended, none of them held a hearing or a vote, so it never reached the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the Expanded & Improved Medicare For All Act on February 3, 2015 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to three committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Natural Resources — and then to subcommittees in February and March 2015 [S5].
That was the last recorded action: no hearing, no committee vote, and no House floor vote occurred before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S1] [S5].
All 62 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers, for-profit hospital operators, and pharmaceutical companies kept the existing market intact, since the bill that would have restructured their industries died in committee without ever being debated on the floor. No new taxes were enacted either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, for-profit hospitals, and drug makers

sides.party_line_note: All 62 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; no Republican cosponsored, and the House's Republican majority controlled the committees that never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill bans private coverage that duplicates the public plan, eliminating the core business of selling comprehensive health insurance. Insurers' revenue comes from collecting premiums and limiting payouts, which is exactly what the bill replaces.

Investor-owned hospitals would have to convert to nonprofit status to participate, with owners paid for losses over 15 years. Their profits come from charging patients and insurers, a source of revenue the single-payer global budgets would remove.

The program would negotiate drug prices annually, buy in bulk, and steer prescribing toward generics, cutting pricing power; universal coverage for all prescriptions would add volume. The net effect depends on how hard the government negotiates.

Hundreds of thousands of clerical, administrative, and billing jobs would be eliminated by the move to a single billing system. The bill acknowledges this directly by funding two years of salary-parity transition benefits and job placement.
